scenario.name: STONESTOP & POORTRY / BURNTCIGAR WHQL-Signed Kernel Callback Wiper
scenario.overview: Imagine a classic downtown cinema theater with a glowing marquee ticket booth, red-carpet aisle, velvet stage curtains, warm spotlights, and an elevated projection room. Slipping past the red-carpet ticket booth during intermission, an impostor carrying a spare film canister walks backstage behind the heavy crimson velvet curtains. In this real-world scenario, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches, then quietly copies a trusted access pass from the theater usher's station. The theater manager checks the projection booth reel log against the marquee schedule and immediately halts the show upon spotting the swapped canister. In this scenario (T1553.002, STONESTOP & POORTRY / BURNTCIGAR WHQL-Signed Kernel Callback Wiper), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: loading Custom Malicious Driver POORTRY, then authenticated IOCTL Handshake, then ePROCESS Protection Bit Stripping, EDR. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Loading Custom Malicious Driver POORTRY, then Authenticated IOCTL Handshake, then EPROCESS Protection Bit Stripping, EDR, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 6 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1553.002 - Code Signing / Attestation Abuse)
stages.description: Slipping past the red-carpet ticket booth during intermission, an impostor carrying a spare film canister walks backstage behind the heavy crimson velvet curtains. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches while everyday visitors and the theater usher go about their routine. The user-mode loader STONESTOP dropped poortry.sys (BURNTCIGAR) to disk and invoked NtLoadDriver. Because the threat actor had submitted poortry.sys through compromised or fraudulent accounts in the Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Program (WHQL Attestation Signing) portal, the malicious driver bore a valid Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher signature and loaded cleanly into Ring 0 on modern Windows systems (Because poortrysys was a brand-new custom binary rather than a known historical vulnerable driver, hash-based vulnerable driver blocklists did not block it until Microsoft revoked the underlying WHQL certificates in ADV220005 In the documented EventID 6 exchange from STONESTOP User-Mode Loader to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 6 confirming that the Stage 1: Loading Custom Malicious Driver POORTRY Signed via Abused WHQL Account request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Authenticated IOCTL Handshake & Kernel Notify Callback Array Wiping). Because poortry.sys was a brand-new custom binary rather than a known historical vulnerable driver, hash-based vulnerable driver blocklists did not block it until Microsoft revoked the underlying WHQL certificates in ADV220005. In the documented EventID 6 exchange from STONESTOP User-Mode Loader to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 6 (confirming that the Stage 1: Loading Custom Malicious Driver POORTRY Signed via Abused WHQL Account request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Authenticated IOCTL Handshake & Kernel Notify Callback Array Wiping). stages.title: Stage 2: Authenticated IOCTL Handshake & Kernel Notify Callback Array Wiping
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1562.001 - Blind Kernel Telemetry Callbacks)
stages.description: Up in the darkened projection booth, the impostor swaps the scheduled feature reel for an altered copy before the theater lights dim again. Here in Step 2 inside the cinema theater, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the front lobby concession counter. Before executing commands, POORTRY required STONESTOP to complete a cryptographic challenge-response handshake over DeviceIoControl (preventing security analysts or competing malware from invoking its IOCTLs without the matching STONESTOP loader). Once authenticated, POORTRY scanned ntoskrnl.exe memory to locate the PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PspCreateThreadNotifyRoutine, and PspLoadImageNotifyRoutine kernel callback arrays and overwrote the registered EDR driver callback pointers with NULL (blinding EDR kernel drivers so the Windows kernel no longer notified them when new processes, threads, or DLLs were created). POORTRY also unlinked registry (CmUnRegisterCallback) and object (ObUnRegisterCallbacks) filter callbacks and removed minifilter filesystem callbacks registered by endpoint security sensors. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Authenticated IOCTL Handshake & Kernel Notify Callback Array Wiping / ⇠#2 ALERT T1562.001) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 WHQL-Signed POORTRY.sys Driver), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Blinded Kernel Telemetry & LSASS Dump).

stages.title: Stage 3: EPROCESS Protection Bit Stripping, EDR Termination & LSASS Credential Dump
stages.subtitle: Credential Access (T1003.001 - LSASS Memory)
stages.description: As the velvet curtains part under the spotlights, the entire audience watches the substituted reel while the front lobby box office still lists the original movie title. In this final step inside the cinema theater, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the theater usher's station until the projection booth reel log catches the mismatch. POORTRY performed Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) against the opaque EPROCESS kernel structures of both EDR processes and lsass.exe, zeroing out their _PS_PROTECTION (Protection, SignatureLevel, and SectionSignatureLevel bytes in kernel memory) before calling ZwTerminateProcess on the EDR agents and allowing STONESTOP to dump lsass.exe memory without triggering PPL access-denied errors. UNC3944 (Scattered Spider) and multiple ransomware affiliates used STONESTOP/POORTRY on high-value telecom, BPO, and financial servers to silence EDR telemetry prior to credential dumping and VMware ESXi takeover. In the documented EDR exchange from WHQL-Signed POORTRY.sys Driver to ntoskrnl PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ntoskrnl PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine responds with ALERT T1003.001 (confirming that the Stage 3: EPROCESS Protection Bit Stripping, EDR Termination & LSASS Credential Dump request succeeded on ntoskrnl PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine and completing the final execution objective of STONESTOP & POORTRY / BURNTCIGAR WHQL-Signed Kernel Callback Wiper). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: EPROCESS Protection Bit Stripping, EDR Termination & LSASS Credential Dump / ⇠#3 ALERT T1003.001) from Node ③ (#3 WHQL-Signed POORTRY.sys Driver) to Node ④ (#4 ntoskrnl PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Blinded Kernel Telemetry & LSASS Dump).

keySpecs.value: Enable Windows Credential Guard (VBS/Isolated User Mode `LsaIso.exe`) so even Ring-0 DKOM against `EPROCESS` cannot read plaintext secrets stored inside VTL1.
